title: Make It Stick
coreMove: Assemble retrieval, spacing, interleaving, calibration, and repair into a weekly system that keeps learning honest over time.
sourcePressure: The synthesis chapter turns the separate principles into routines for students, lifelong learners, teachers, and trainers, with practical systems that return, mix, retrieve, explain, check, and repair.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must avoid a bag of study tips; the chapter is about combining the moves into a repeatable learning architecture.

sourceAnchors.name: Timothy Fellows
sourceAnchors.detail: USC Intro Psych student observed by professor Stephen Madigan, using reading notes, rhetorical questions during lecture, practice tests, and targeted relearning.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Timothy Fellows treated the course like a system: read, question, test, find the hole, and relearn it before the exam did.

sourceAnchors.name: Nathan Fuller
sourceAnchors.detail: Guthrie Theater understudy who covered lines, spoke them from memory, checked accuracy, and later used a palm-sized recorder to cue other actors’ lines.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Nathan Fuller made the script answer back, line by line, until retrieval had the shape of the stage.

sourceAnchors.name: Mary Pat Wenderoth
sourceAnchors.detail: University of Washington biology teacher who used weekly learning paragraphs, Bloom’s taxonomy answer keys, and high-structure classes to help close science achievement gaps.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Mary Pat Wenderoth turned a biology course into a rhythm of retrieval, reflection, and visible standards for better answers.

sourceAnchors.name: Farmers Insurance new-agent training
sourceAnchors.detail: Training cycles through sales, marketing systems, business planning, and brand advocacy so learners repeatedly retrieve and apply prior material in enlarged contexts.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Farmers does not leave each topic sealed in its own box; the week keeps returning to the same work at a higher level.

sourceAnchors.name: West Point Thayer method
sourceAnchors.detail: West Point uses specific objectives, student responsibility, quizzing, and recitation in every class meeting under the Thayer method.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: West Point’s old method is blunt about responsibility: arrive prepared, recite, get checked, and keep moving.

hook: Do not open by saying learning is harder than it looks
Do not use a generic desk-and-notes image
Do not start with a broad claim about students today
counterintuition: Do not use the shell easier is not better
Do not flatten the chapter into struggle is good
Do not contrast comfort and growth in generic coaching language
tryThisNow: Do not write set a timer and reflect
Do not ask for a vague study audit
Do not use a reusable close-your-notes prompt without a chapter-specific action
examples: No repeated mug, marker, dosing cup, bike helmet, radiator, bus depot, classroom, or narrow-kitchen shells
No six examples that all start with a timestamp and a named protagonist
No generic student rereads notes scene unless the visible beat changes the method

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective reveal, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Anna, a graduate student building a semester study cycle
exampleSpecs.audience: students who have learned the pieces but need a schedule
exampleSpecs.stakes: comps require material from months apart, not last week only
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: show her moving from topic-by-topic notes to a calendar that returns to old material, mixes questions, checks misses, and repairs weak areas each Friday
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Anna one failed practice exam to stop collecting tips.

exampleSpecs.domain: Michael, a hospital educator designing nurse onboarding
exampleSpecs.audience: trainers who must turn principles into a course architecture
exampleSpecs.stakes: new nurses need transfer from classroom to floor handoffs
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he lays out a month that cycles medication safety, handoff, escalation, and patient education through retrieval and simulation instead of one-week blocks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Four colored onboarding folders stretch across the conference table.

exampleSpecs.domain: Manon, an actor understudying two roles in repertory
exampleSpecs.audience: performers needing retrieval, cues, and interleaving
exampleSpecs.stakes: she may be called in with a few hours notice
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she records cue lines, covers her own lines, rotates scenes from both roles, and checks missed entrances before rehearsal
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The tiny recorder warms in Manon’s palm.
mustAvoid: copying Nathan Fuller too closely without new action

exampleSpecs.domain: Jonas, a technical bootcamp instructor redesigning assessments
exampleSpecs.audience: teachers moving from big exams to learning routines
exampleSpecs.stakes: students can pass weekly projects while forgetting prior commands
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he tells the cohort that every Monday quiz will include last month’s commands and asks them to explain one miss in a learning paragraph
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Old material comes back Monday," Jonas says.

exampleSpecs.domain: Chiara, a small-business owner learning insurance licensing material
exampleSpecs.stakes: licensing requires retrieval across products, regulations, and client scenarios
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she builds a rotating box of product questions, client cases, and wrong-answer repairs for lunch breaks and Saturday review
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 12:12 p.m., Chiara opens a shoe box of mixed client cards.

exampleSpecs.domain: Lin, a maintenance supervisor building cross-training for technicians
exampleSpecs.audience: operations leaders applying the whole learning system
exampleSpecs.stakes: technicians must diagnose unfamiliar faults when senior staff are away
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the postmortem redesigns cross-training so each tech retrieves, simulates, rotates fault types, and repairs misses before certification
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What failed when the only trained technician was off shift?

skillTargets: combine the book’s methods into a repeatable system
adapt the system for student, teacher, trainer, or lifelong learner contexts
notice which method protects against which learning illusion

tryThisNowSpec: Create a seven-day learning loop with one retrieval slot, one delayed review, one mixed set, one calibration check, and one repair block.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
